title: I can't stop worrying
seoTitle: Can't Stop Worrying? Anxiety, the Bible, and What Helps
description: Anxiety is not a verdict on your faith. What's happening in body and soul, what Scripture says about worry, and what to do this week.
summary: For the worry that won't switch off: what's happening, what Scripture says, and what to do tonight and this week.
askedAs: What does the Bible say about anxiety
answer: You lie down tired and your mind starts working anyway: the bill, the test results, the child, the thing you said, the thing that might happen next. Your heart runs faster than the room deserves. You've prayed, and the loop is still running, and under the worry sits a second fear, that a stronger Christian would be free of this by now. Anxiety is not a verdict on your faith. It's a weight on body and soul together, more common in church than anyone lets on, and it deserves real care, from God and from people. Tonight, put the worries on paper and leave the list by your bed; you don't have to solve them before morning. If the fear has turned into thoughts of not wanting to be alive, don't wait for morning: call or text 988, or use the lines just below.
happening:
Worry is the mind trying to solve tomorrow tonight. It picks up a problem, turns it over, finds no handle, sets it down, and picks it up again. The same loop can run backward, replaying the thing you said or the thing you should have done, and counselors call that rumination. Both are hard to stop because they feel responsible, as if thinking about a danger were the same as doing something about it. The loop rarely produces a decision. It produces another lap.

Anxiety is what happens when the body joins in. The heart speeds up, breathing turns shallow, the stomach knots, the shoulders climb, and sleep goes first. It can be a dread with no object, or a jolt awake at three in the morning with the alarm already ringing. It can crest into panic: a sudden surge of terror, a pounding heart, shaking, a sense of unreality or of dying, then exhaustion and the fear of the next one. Sometimes it fits what's happening, a layoff or a diagnosis; other times it has outgrown its cause, or has no cause you can find. Both are real.

Each common explanation gets something right. Doctors are right that this is physical: your body has an alarm built to protect you, and in anxiety it rings when there's no fire, or keeps ringing after the fire is out. Sleep, illness, hormones, medications, caffeine, and alcohol all turn it up or down, which is one reason to see a doctor. Counselors would add that habits of thought matter: the mind learns to scan for danger and rehearse the worst, avoidance teaches the fear that it was right, and hard histories set the alarm to go off sooner. And the church is right that worry has something to do with trust; Scripture speaks to it often, and tenderly.

Taken alone, though, each leaves you smaller than you are. The medical account can make your fear a malfunction with no meaning, when some of what you fear deserves your care. The psychological account can forget that you're a creature with real limits, trying to carry what no creature can. And the church's version, as it's often handed out, leaves the body out and turns a symptom into a sin, so the anxious person ends up with two problems, the fear and the shame of the fear. You are one person, body and soul, and help usually comes from several directions at once.

scripture.intro: Scripture gives anxious people words, and it doesn't edit their fear out. Each passage below is read in its setting: a prisoner writing to friends he couldn't visit, Jesus teaching people who lived on daily bread, a betrayed man praying for wings to fly away, and a letter to Christians under pressure.

passages.text: Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.
passages.reading: Paul wrote this in custody, “in chains for Christ” (Philippians 1:13), unsure whether he would live or die, in a letter that keeps returning to joy. The church there had begun, in part, on the night he and Silas, beaten and locked in stocks in the city's jail, were heard “praying and singing hymns to God” at midnight, and the jailer and his household believed before the night was over (Acts 16:25-34). The verse asks you to bring everything to God, by name, with thanks for what is still true. The word for anxious here is the one Paul used to praise Timothy, who would “genuinely care for your needs” (Philippians 2:20); care is no sin, and the question is where you carry it. Then comes a promise. Paul's word for guard is a soldier's word: God's peace will stand over your heart and mind the way a garrison stands over a city. It surpasses understanding, so you don't have to reason your way into it, and you can be kept before you feel calm.

passages.text: Therefore do not worry, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ For the Gentiles strive after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them. But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added unto you. Therefore do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Today has enough trouble of its own.
passages.reading: Jesus said this to his disciples, with crowds of ordinary people listening (Matthew 5:1; 7:28), many of them living hand to mouth. They had just been taught to pray, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11). The question of what to eat was real. The reason he gives is that “your heavenly Father knows that you need them” (Matthew 6:32): he answers fear by telling you who is paying attention. He's honest about the day, too. “Today has enough trouble of its own” (Matthew 6:34) admits the trouble, then draws a line around it, because worry borrows tomorrow's trouble and pays for it tonight. He does say, “O you of little faith” (Matthew 6:30), and anxious readers tend to hear nothing else. Elsewhere in Matthew the phrase goes to frightened disciples in a storm (Matthew 8:26), and when Peter began to sink, Jesus said it with his hand already holding him (Matthew 14:31).

passages.text: My heart murmurs within me, and the terrors of death assail me. Fear and trembling grip me, and horror has overwhelmed me. I said, “Oh, that I had wings like a dove! I would fly away and find rest. How far away I would flee! In the wilderness I would remain. Selah I would hurry to my shelter, far from this raging tempest.”
passages.reading: The psalm carries David's name, and its trouble is betrayal by “my companion and close friend” (Psalm 55:13) in a city full of violence. What he describes reads like panic: a heart in anguish, terror, trembling, horror, and the wish to get far away from all of it. He brings it to God without tidying it first, and God kept that prayer in Scripture for every frightened person who would ever run out of words. The psalm circles; the fear and the anger keep coming back. But in the middle David says, “Morning, noon, and night, I cry out in distress, and He hears my voice” (Psalm 55:17). He never gets the wings he asked for. He gets a hearing. And near the end he turns to whoever is listening: “Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you” (Psalm 55:22).

passages.text: Humble yourselves, therefore, under God’s mighty hand, so that in due time He may exalt you. Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.
passages.reading: The letter comes in Peter's name to scattered Christians in what is now Turkey, slandered by their neighbors and facing what it calls “the fiery trial” (1 Peter 4:12). In the Greek, the word for cast in verse 7 depends on the command to humble yourselves in verse 6, so handing over your anxiety is part of how you bow under God's mighty hand: you admit the load is too heavy and set it down where it belongs. Peter is also borrowing from Psalm 55. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament the early church read, the psalm's line about casting your burden on the LORD uses the same two words Peter uses here, cast and anxiety. He takes a sentence from a frightened man's prayer and hands it to frightened churches, with one reason attached: “He cares for you.”

whyHard:
It's natural to assume the problem is you: your wiring, your willpower, your faith. Some of that is true; bodies and histories differ, and some people carry a quicker alarm through no fault of their own. But your worry is also the weather of a whole culture, and most of us have been standing out in it for years.

The body was made to respond to danger it could see: a storm coming in, a stranger at the door, a sick child in the next room. Now the whole world's dangers arrive in a pocket, all day, through feeds built to hold our attention, and few things hold attention like alarm. The body rings the same bell for the screen as for the room. We know about more dangers than any people before us and can act on almost none of them, and worry lives in that gap. Add a life that is always watched and compared, and even a Tuesday starts to feel like a performance under review.

Then the limits went. Scripture writes them into the world from its first page: evening and morning, work and rest, six days and a seventh. Deuteronomy grounds the Sabbath in memory: “Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 5:15). In Egypt the brick quota never went down, and when the Hebrews asked for time to worship, Pharaoh's answer was “Make the work harder on the men so they will be occupied” (Exodus 5:9). Free people stop, and their rest confesses that the world doesn't depend on them. We kept the quota and dropped the stop. The phone comes to bed, and the office and the news come with it. A mind never allowed to put anything down will pick everything up, usually in the dark.

Underneath both lies something heavier. Modern people are told in a hundred ways that we belong to ourselves. We choose our work, our beliefs, our identity, and our meaning, then keep choosing and defending them, because nothing is given and nothing is settled. There's real freedom in that, and I wouldn't want a world where a life was fixed at birth. But a self that has to make itself never gets to rest. Kierkegaard, who wrote a whole book on the subject in 1844, described anxiety as the dizziness that comes with freedom itself, the vertigo of a creature looking down into everything it might become. If everything depends on you, of course you're awake at three in the morning. Someone has to hold the world together, and you've been told it's you.

The church should have been the place to set that weight down, and too often we added to it. We made peace a proof of faith and calm a sign of maturity, so anxious believers learned to perform serenity on Sunday and hide the rest, and we quoted Philippians 4:6 at them like a charge sheet. I count myself inside this. Pastors reach for a verse because it's faster than sitting down beside someone, and because another person's fear can frighten us. Some of that came from real love and a real taste of God's peace; some came from a faith that had absorbed the culture's logic, where trust is one more job that falls on you. The skeptic calls religion a sedative for frightened people, and religion used that way has earned the charge. The Psalms make a poor sedative. They keep their fear on the page.

The older faith had already answered this burden. The Heidelberg Catechism, published in 1563 to teach the young and to guide preaching in the churches, opens by asking what our only comfort is in life and in death, and answers that we are not our own; we belong, body and soul, to Christ. Paul had said it first: “You are not your own; you were bought at a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). That sentence won't switch off an alarm. It moves the weight. Scripture says of Christ that “in Him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:17). Someone is holding the world together tonight. It was never supposed to be you.

thisWeek.intro: None of this is a cure, and none of it has to be done well to count. Start with the first step tonight, and if the worry has lasted for weeks, don't skip the last.

steps.title: Name it on paper
steps.body: Worry feeds on vagueness. Write down what you're afraid of, as specifically as you can: the bill, the scan, the conversation, the thing you can't name yet. Beside each one, write one thing you can do about it this week. Where there's nothing to do, mark it as something only God can carry, and let that part of the list become your prayer. Keep the paper by your bed, and when the loop starts at night, add to the list instead of arguing with it.

steps.title: Give your body a fair chance
steps.body: You're one person, so before you ask your soul to be calm, look after your body. Keep regular hours for sleep, eat real meals, and walk outside in daylight. Notice honestly what caffeine and alcohol do to your sleep and your nerves. When the alarm rises, slow your breathing and make each breath out longer than the breath in. When the prophet Elijah lay down spent under a broom tree, God let him sleep and fed him, twice, before the word of the LORD came to him with a question (1 Kings 19:5-9).

steps.title: Turn down the alarms
steps.body: For one week, limit what sets the alarm off. Turn off news and social media notifications. Check the headlines once a day, well before bed. Charge your phone outside the bedroom and buy a cheap alarm clock if you need one. The world's trouble will still be there in the morning, and you'll meet it better rested. At the end of the week, notice what your mind did with the room you gave it.

steps.title: Pray a psalm out loud
steps.body: Open to Psalm 55, or Psalms 42 and 43, and read one aloud as your own prayer. Don't tidy yourself up first; the psalmists didn't. Ask with them, “Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me?” (Psalm 42:5). If your mind keeps turning over things too big for it, pray Psalm 131, three short verses in which a soul is quieted “like a weaned child with his mother” (Psalm 131:2). You don't have to feel anything for this to count as prayer.

steps.title: Tell one person
steps.body: Anxiety grows in hiding. Choose one person you trust, a friend, a parent, your spouse, a pastor, and tell them plainly: *I've been more anxious than I've let on, and I don't want to carry it alone anymore.* You don't need to explain it well. Ask them to check on you once this week. If there's no one to tell, say that to a doctor or a pastor; being alone with it makes everything louder.

steps.title: Make the appointment
steps.body: If the worry has been steady for weeks, or it's taking your sleep, your work, or your joy, call this week and book a visit with your doctor or a licensed counselor. A doctor can check whether something physical is feeding the alarm and talk with you about treatment; a counselor can teach your mind new habits for the loop. Going is an act of faith in a God who works through ordinary means.

moreHelp.body:
Anxiety is more than a pastoral matter when it shows the signs below, and it's urgent the moment the fear turns into thoughts of not wanting to be alive. You don't have to be thinking about suicide to call or text 988; it's also there for a night when the fear won't let go.

A good first step is often your regular doctor, who can look for physical causes, talk with you about treatment, and refer you to a counselor. You can also find a licensed counselor, psychologist, or clinical social worker through your insurance plan's directory, or ask a pastor which counselors in your area people trust. Confirm that the counselor is licensed in your state; most state licensing boards let you check online. If you want a Christian counselor, ask about their training and how their faith shapes their work. Shared faith is worth looking for, and it never replaces a license.

If a doctor recommends medication, taking it is not faithlessness. I'm a pastor, not a physician, and nothing here is medical advice. But I'd rather you make that call this week than read one more page about worry, this one included.
signs: You're having thoughts of not wanting to be alive, or that others would be better off without you. Call or text 988 now.
Chest pain, trouble breathing, or fainting that no doctor has checked: get care right away, and call 911 if you need to.
Panic attacks keep coming, or fear of the next one decides where you go.
You've slept badly most nights for more than two weeks.
You're relying on alcohol, pills, or anything else to calm down or to sleep.
The worry is costing you work, school, or the people you love, or your life is shrinking around what you avoid.

You're afraid of someone at home who hurts, threatens, or controls you. That's a safety matter before it's an anxiety one: the Domestic Violence Hotline above can help you make a safety plan, and 911 is for immediate danger.
moreHelp.firstCall: You don't have to tell your whole story on the phone. To a doctor's office it can be as simple as: *I've been dealing with a lot of anxiety for a while, it's affecting my sleep and my work, and I'd like an appointment to talk about it.* With a counselor, ask whether they're taking new clients, whether they take your insurance or offer a reduced fee, whether they have experience with anxiety, and whether they're licensed in your state. If calling feels impossible, many offices let you book online, or a friend can sit beside you while you call.
moreHelp.cost: Cost shouldn't be the reason you go without care. Check your insurance first; many plans cover doctor visits and counseling. If you're uninsured or the copay is too high, ask counselors about sliding-scale fees, look for a community mental health center, or call a nearby university with a counseling or psychology graduate program, since many run training clinics where supervised students see clients at lower cost. If you're employed, ask about an employee assistance program, which often covers a few sessions at no charge. And tell your pastor; some churches keep a benevolence fund for exactly this.

helping.body:
If you love someone who is anxious, know first that you can't argue them out of it. Anxiety isn't mainly a problem of logic, and endless reassurance usually buys an hour of relief and a longer loop. What helps is steadier: your presence, your patience, and your willingness to stay in the room while the fear is loud.

Anxious people often feel like a burden, so they hide it, and what you see may look like irritability, withdrawal, or constant checking. Offer practical help, because anxiety makes small tasks feel enormous: drive them to the appointment, sit beside them while they make the call, take one thing off their list.

If you're a parent, your child borrows calm from your face; stay near the fear without feeding it, and talk to your child's doctor if the worry is steady or shrinking their world. If you're a pastor or group leader, don't treat anxiety as a discipline problem; pray with the person, and keep a short list of licensed counselors you trust so you can refer the same week. And if someone you're helping says anything about not wanting to be alive, ask directly whether they're thinking about suicide. Asking plainly won't put the idea in their head, and it may be the first time anyone has let them say it.
say: You don't have to explain it for me to take it seriously.
What would help most right now: company, quiet, or a walk?
Do you want me to come with you to the appointment?
helping.next: Follow up. Send the text tomorrow, and again the day after. Help with whatever practical step they're stuck on, whether that's finding a counselor or making the call. If they tell you they're thinking about suicide, stay with them and call or text 988 together, or call 911 if they're in immediate danger. Then get support for yourself; loving an anxious person is heavy. Parents will find more in [How to Help an Anxious Child](/how-tos/parenting-how-to-help-an-anxious-child).

prayer:
Father, it's late, and my mind won't stop. I've run the same list a hundred times and it hasn't gotten shorter. My heart won't slow down, and I'm tired of being afraid.

I won't pretend with you. You know what I'm carrying and what I'm afraid of losing. I can't hold tomorrow. I've been trying, and it's crushing me. So I'm setting it down in front of you, one thing at a time, including the thing I haven't told anyone.

You said you care for me. I can't feel it tonight. Be true to your word anyway. Guard my heart and my mind when I can't guard them. You never slumber or sleep, so let me sleep. And if sleep won't come, hear me the way you heard David when he wanted to fly away.

Give me one person to tell, and the nerve to tell them. Give me the humility to take the help you send, whether it comes through a friend, a doctor, or a psalm someone else wrote.

When morning comes, let me be your creature again: small, fed, held, and not in charge of the world. You are. In Jesus' name, amen.

Anxiety and the Peace of Christ

faq.a: Feeling anxious is not a sin. David's heart churned with terror (Psalm 55:4-5), and the night before the cross Jesus himself was “sorrowful and deeply distressed” (Matthew 26:37). Trust and fear can live in the same person on the same night; the Psalms are full of people who trusted God and were still afraid. Scripture does call us to bring our worries to God instead of carrying them alone, and Jesus warns that worry gets tangled up with what we trust, money especially (Matthew 6:24-25). But “Be anxious for nothing” (Philippians 4:6) comes with an invitation to pray and a promise of peace. If you were taught that anxiety proves weak faith, that teaching added a weight God never asked you to carry.

faq.q: Is it wrong for a Christian to take anxiety medication?
faq.a: No. Taking medication a doctor has prescribed is not a failure of faith, any more than taking insulin or wearing glasses is. Christians have long received medicine as one of God's ordinary gifts; Paul called his companion Luke “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14). Whether medication is right for you is a medical question for you and your doctor, and many people are helped by counseling, medication, or both. Don't start, stop, or change a medication on your own. And keep praying while you take it; prayer and medicine have never been rivals.

faq.q: Why is my anxiety worse at night?
faq.a: At night the distractions fall away, your body is tired, and nothing can be done about any problem until morning, so the mind rehearses instead of acting, and worries look larger in the dark. Keep paper by the bed and write the worry down, keep the phone and the news out of the bedroom, and pray a short psalm: “I will lie down and sleep in peace, for You alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety” (Psalm 4:8). If you're waking in fear most nights, or barely sleeping for weeks, tell your doctor.

faq.q: What should I do during a panic attack?
faq.a: If you've never had this checked, or you aren't sure whether it's your heart or something else, get medical help right away, and call 911 if you need to; there's no shame in that call. If a doctor has already told you these are panic attacks, remember what's happening: your body's alarm is sounding at full volume, and the surge will crest and pass even when it feels as if it won't. Slow your breathing, with a longer breath out than in. Feel your feet on the floor. Pray in a few words, *Lord, help me*, and let that be enough. Afterward, tell your doctor or counselor; panic can be treated.

You usually can't stop a thought by fighting it head-on; arguing with a worry tends to feed it. Change what you do with it instead. Write it down and decide whether there's one thing you can do about it this week. If there isn't, hand it to God in plain words, then give your mind something else to hold: a walk, work with your hands, a conversation with someone who isn't worried. If overthinking fills your days, a counselor can teach you practical ways to interrupt the loop.

faq.q: What Bible verses help with anxiety?
faq.a: Start with the passages on this page: Philippians 4:6-7, Matthew 6:25-34, Psalm 55, and 1 Peter 5:6-7. Then add Psalm 94:19, “When anxiety overwhelms me, Your consolation delights my soul,” which admits the anxiety comes; Psalm 131, a quieting prayer; Psalm 4:8 for the night; Isaiah 41:10, “Do not fear, for I am with you”; and Psalms 42 and 43, which ask the soul why it is downcast and keep asking. Read each in its whole chapter, as a prayer rather than a pill. They're there to give you words when you bring your fear to God.

Truth: every quotation in the prose was checked with node scripts/bsb.mjs against the verse it cites (the validator only confirms the words occur somewhere in the BSB), and all match. Sources re-checked through search-engine excerpts, because direct fetches are blocked from this environment: 988 (you don't have to be suicidal to call); Dazzi, Gribble, Wessely, and Fear, Psychological Medicine 44, no. 16 (2014): 3361-3363 (no reviewed study found a significant rise in suicidal ideation from being asked); the Heidelberg Catechism (approved January 1563, for teaching the young and guiding preaching; the page now says published, not written, in 1563); Kierkegaard's The Concept of Anxiety (1844, anxiety as the dizziness of freedom; the SEP entry carries the passage); Philippians 2:20 and 4:6 share merimnao; phroureo in 4:7 is a military guard word (source added); the participle in 1 Peter 5:7 depends on 5:6; 1 Peter 5:7 echoes Septuagint Psalm 54:23 (cast, anxiety). Changes: the Philippians reading no longer implies that particular readers of the letter believed at the jail (the church began partly that night, Acts 16:25-34); the 1 Peter reading states the grammatical dependence and calls casting part of how you humble yourself, instead of asserting one reading of the participle; rumination now names the backward loop, as counselors use the word; a generic first-person line about being awake at three in the morning became second person so it cannot be read as James's own experience; the Elijah line now follows 1 Kings 19:5-9 (the angel spoke first; the word of the LORD came at Horeb); the soul no longer lives in the body; the answer now gives the midnight reader one thing to do tonight.
